claims.text: Wear performance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is governed by formation of a stable, coherent, and dense surface oxide layer.
The properties of the surface oxide layer are determined by alloy composition and microstructure.
Changing principal-element ratios or coating microstructure will alter the surface oxide layer.
The relevant structural mediator is a stable, coherent, and dense oxide layer formed on the coating surface.
The oxide layer acts as a barrier to wear and corrosion.
The oxide barrier reduces wear rate and improves coating durability.
Optimizing composition or microstructure is expected to reduce wear rate by 20–50% relative to a non-optimized baseline coating.
The baseline non-optimized high-entropy-alloy coating exhibits a wear rate of 10^-4 mm^3/Nm.
The hypothesis should apply to multiple-principal-element high-entropy alloys such as AlCoCrFeNi.
The hypothesis should hold under loads of 10–100 N and sliding speeds of 0.1–10 m/s.
The exact relationship between composition or microstructure and oxide-layer properties is not well understood.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to all high-entropy alloys or wear applications.
A lack of statistically significant correlation between composition or microstructure and wear rate, using p > 0.05, would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure of oxide-layer properties to vary with composition or microstructure would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis says that oxide-layer formation governs wear, but the falsification rule tests only composition/microstructure correlations. It does not directly require oxide-layer properties to correlate with wear, so it could reject or retain the hypothesis without testing the stated mediator-to-outcome relationship.
